nodes.title: S U M M A R Y
nodes.summary: A 1956 report summarizing a research contract for an aircraft using propulsive jets for stabilization and control. Covers design progress, a proposed prototype, feasibility and performance studies showing whole-flight handling from ground-cushion takeoff to supersonic flight (Mach 3-4, ceiling over 100,000 ft, range about 1,000 nautical miles), needed further tests, production aspects, a broader follow-on program outline, and a cost estimate of $3,168,000 over 18 to 24 months.

nodes.title: 2 " I N T R O D U C T I O N
nodes.summary: Avro Aircraft Project 1794 final report (June 1956) on a limited feasibility contract for a flat, vertical take-off and landing aircraft. Covers air cushion effect, multi-engine stability, air intake and exhaust testing, performance/stability/control, and radial-flow engine feasibility. Describes design evolution from radial turbojet and wheel-spoke concepts to a ducted-fan circular planform with a thin wing, now adopted, with construction proceeding.

nodes.title: 4 . P R O J E C T 7 0 4
4. ID e s c r i p t i o n
nodes.summary: Describes Avro Aircraft Project 704 (1956), a VTOL jet aircraft about 35.3 ft in diameter and 7.7 ft tall, with six Viper turbojets driving contra-rotating centrifugal impellers that force air through the wing. Covers the weight and fuel figures, exhaust-jet control via shutters for vertical takeoff, hover, maneuvering and pitch stabilization, and the centre-of-gravity position at mid-wing chord relative to stability.

nodes.title: 4. Z Operation
nodes.summary: Describes the Avro Aircraft Project 1794 vertical take-off concept. Take-off: shutters on the wing underside open and about 20,000 lb of downward jet thrust without afterburning creates a ground cushion, raising lift to possibly 30,000 lb and lifting the aircraft to about 20 feet. Transition to forward flight uses a transition control to lean jets backward. Forward flight uses ram pressure into the intake, supersonic augmentation, high thrust-to-weight, high ceiling, and forecast long supersonic range. Landing is a vertical descent or steep approach, then jets are transferred to the underside and leaned forward to decelerate, nose lowered to hover, and throttle closed on touchdown. Fig. 8 shows the ground cushion effect.

nodes.title: 4 . 3Perforrnance
nodes.summary: Performance summary for the first prototype of Avro Project 1794 VTOL aircraft (June 1956), initially restricted by a Mach number limit on Viper engines. Assuming the restriction is removed, at 1200K main combustion temperature it lists: maximum level speed Mach 2.0 (94,000 ft); supersonic ceiling; altitude for normal acceleration of 7.33g in steady turn at 53,000 ft; still-air range on full internal fuel, including take-off climb and acceleration allowances, of about 1,000 nautical miles cruising at Mach 2.25 at 90,000 ft. Also a continuation section on take-off and landing.

title: 5 . DISCUSSION OF ACTIVITIES

nodes.title: 5 . DISCUSSION OF ACTIVITIES (intro)
nodes.summary: A 1956 Avro Aircraft Project 1794 (Stability and Control Model No. 2/16) report section on wind tunnel tests. Subsonic tests on a 1/6 scale reflection-plane model (500+ hours, 34 weeks at Wright Air Development Centre) covered ground effect, transition, and in-flight control, with intake/exhaust simulation. Findings: controllable takeoff/landing and transition, poor subsonic cruise efficiency due to high drag, and need for further transition, pressure, control, hot-jet, and intake tests. Supersonic tests (76 hours at MIT NSL) on three models found good control, drag agreeing with estimates, better-than-expected cruise efficiency and intake recovery, with further testing needed for intake-running drag, broader data, and transonic tests.

nodes.title: P RO f EC T t 7 9 4
P RO f EC T t 7 9 4 (intro)
nodes.summary: Avro Aircraft Project 1794 (VTOL air intake boundary-layer bleeding) reports small-scale tests: a simple cusp below the air entry improved by shape variants; subsonic and supersonic jet-trim, transition, and dynamic rate/displacement stability model tests (Figs. 31-37); and air intake internal flow models (Figs. 38-39). Preliminary tests justified a larger program. Static internal flow showed satisfactory pressure recovery; forward flight recovery was satisfactory but flow distribution to the impeller eye was poor, needing larger-scale tests and possibly radial cascades and pre-swirl. Air cushion tests at Malton on 10-inch and 20-inch models showed ground lift augmentation up to 1.8 times jet thrust at 45 percent span, falling rapidly outboard, and sensitivity to jet angle, aspect ratio, intake, exhaust, and lower surface shape.

nodes.title: stability and controlTests:
stability and controlTests: (intro)
nodes.summary: A 1956 Avro Aircraft Project 1794 report section on stability and control. Wind tunnel tests gathered aerodynamic data. Further needed: transonic aerodynamic and control data via a new force model with intake and exhaust jet simulation, and rig tests of the pneumatic system and shutters, especially response speed. A simple rig with one nozzle pair was built (Fig. 47) to get response data and develop shutter control. The contractor plans a peripheral segment attached to the central test piece, described in section 8. The contract called for six-component data, but the models measure only lift, drag and pitching moment, since side force, rolling and yawing moments are secondary for this symmetrical design.

summary: A 1956 Avro Project 1794 wind tunnel report. Subsonic tests (1/6 scale, 500+ hours) covered ground effect, transition, control, and intake/exhaust simulation: takeoff/landing and transition controllable, subsonic cruise drag poor, more tests needed. Supersonic tests (76 hours, MIT) showed good control, drag matching estimates, better cruise and intake recovery; intake drag and transonic tests pending. Small-scale intake tests: static pressure recovery satisfactory, forward-flight flow poor, air cushion lift augmentation up to 1.8x, nozzle thrust recovery about 60%.

nodes.title: 5 . r . 4 . 3 (Co nt' d ) (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes a 1956 Avro Aircraft report (Project 1794) on a right-angle bend thrust recovery test using a ground-effect balance, with a proposed 1/3 scale nozzle end-loss test; wind tunnel performance tests; a theoretical ground cushion effect estimate; stability and control analyses (longitudinal, lateral, pneumatic control time constant, hovering) concluding the proposed system can give conventional flying qualities; air intake and exhaust analyses; aircraft performance estimates with drag confirmed by supersonic tests; and radial flow propulsion design study figures.

nodes.title: 5.2.5 Radial Flow Feasibility:
nodes.summary: Avro Aircraft Project 704 report (June 1956, section 5.2): states aircraft performance estimates across development stages (thrust/drag, superior to earlier designs, supersonic-test confirmed). Section 5.2.5 covers radial flow propulsion feasibility: three rejected configurations (ducted fan with Viper engines, centrifugal impeller with Rolls-Royce R.B.108 gas generators, reduction-gear design), then Project 704's Viper engines laid flat in the wing driving split centrifugal impellers via radial inflow turbines, with high-bypass (5:1) pressurized intakes. Fig. 56 compares four methods of 12,000 lb vertical lift by horsepower versus mass flow.

summary: Avro Aircraft 1956 report (Projects 1794/704): right-angle bend thrust recovery test with ground-effect balance and proposed 1/3 scale nozzle end-loss test; wind tunnel performance; ground cushion estimate; longitudinal, lateral, pneumatic control and hovering stability analyses concluding conventional flying qualities; intake and exhaust analyses; performance estimates confirmed by supersonic tests. Radial flow feasibility: rejected ducted fan, centrifugal and gear designs; adopted wing-mounted Viper engines driving split impellers via radial turbines with 5:1 bypass intakes. Fig. 56 compares four 12,000 lb lift methods.

title: 6 . T A B U L A T E D L A B O U R & C O S T S U M M A R Y
summary: Avro Aircraft Project 1794 Tabulated Labour and Costs Summary (July 1, 1954 to June 1, 1956). Covers manhours and costs by investigation area: air cushion effect, stability and control, air intake and gas exhaust, airplane performance, and radial flow/hild analysis, split into engineering and manufacturing. Totals about $453,897.77 spent, leaving a balance of about $287,921.22 of funds, expected to cover remaining reports through June 1956. Includes charts 1-6.

title: 7 . DEVELOPMENT AND PRODUCTION ASPECTS
summary: Project 704 is cheaper to manufacture than conventional aircraft due to symmetry and repetition: six identical segments, each with a Viper engine, built in one jig (about 90% of the airframe), reducing tooling, design, and development time. A single prototype is to be built first, flown cold without outer combustion, then fitted with combustion to reach supersonic speed, limited to Mach 1.74 by the Viper. Later prototypes may use other engines and be all steel. The first prototype uses steel outer wing and rotors, with a light alloy center. A test programme follows.

title: 8 . N E W P R O G R A M S R E Q U I R E D

nodes.title: 8 . N E W P R O G R A M S R E Q U I R E D (intro)
nodes.summary: Avro Aircraft Project 1794 (June 1956) lists new test programs: wind tunnel tests (supersonic 1/23 scale force model with transonic half-plane model, subsonic 1/6 scale model in 20 ft Massie tunnel, internal air intake flow half-model, nozzle end loss model, small-scale tests), ground effect tests with a 1/20 scale jet model, internal flow tests (air intake, single engine intake/exhaust with Viper engine), a full-scale 6-Viper propulsion system test rig with fuel, fire protection and control systems, an oscillation rig and shutter box, and an outer wing segment and control system. Tunnel time estimates and cost forecasts are included.
